card.hook: Picture a three-faced clock tower sitting on top of a market with nearly 1,500 booths, and traffic swirling around it like it's the middle of a very loud roundabout. That's Bến Thành, and yes, it's as photogenic as the postcards say.
card.stand_here: Stand in Quảng trường Quách Thị Trang, the open square opposite the South Gate, and face the clock tower. You'll get the tower in front with the long market facade spreading out behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the tower with the facade behind it. If the square is crowded or you're close, tap 0.5x to fit the whole frontage in. Try 2x or more (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the clock face.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the clock tower, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out the facade.
card.best_time: Go early, before about 8 AM, when the facade looks cleaner and fewer people wander across your view. In the evening, the stalls on Phan Bội Châu and Phan Châu Trinh light up, so switch on night mode for a lively scene.
card.selfie_here: Use the pedestrian area in front of the South Gate facade on Lê Lợi Street, opposite Quách Thị Trang Park. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if you have it), then tilt up slightly so the clock tower sits over your shoulder. One guide says the city has closed this area to traffic for photographers, but check when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Quách Thị Trang traffic circle facing the South Gate and shoot toward the yellow clock tower, while you pose in front of the gate.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask vendors before taking close-up photos of them or their goods. Traffic is heavy here, so watch your back when you step back or pose for photos.
card.challenge: Can you get the clock tower dead centre on the gridlines with nobody walking through the frame? Bonus points if you wait for exactly one person to stroll past.
card.good_to_know: The market moved into this building in 1912. It covers about 13,056 square metres, and the French Indochinese-style roof lines were designed to give shade and natural airflow. The exterior has had a refresh, so it may look different from older travel photos.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Quảng trường Quách Thị Trang, the open square opposite the South Gate, and face the clock tower. You'll get the tower in front with the long market facade spreading out behind it.

card.hook: Picture a street where every shopfront is trying to out-glow the one next door, and the crowd is part of the show. That's Bùi Viện after dark, and your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the east entrance gate, where Bùi Viện meets Trần Hưng Đạo Boulevard, about 143 m to the north-east of the crossroads drop-off. Face west, look under the entrance arch and along the street into the neon.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the arch and the street ahead. If the pavement is packed and you can't step back, try 0.5x, or go to 2x to pick out the signs and pull the far end closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the scene, then slide it a little darker so the neon keeps its colour instead of turning white.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the signs are lit and the street is busy. Saturday and Sunday evenings from 7 pm the street is closed to vehicles, so those are the easiest for walking and framing, but check locally as arrangements can change.
card.selfie_here: Stand beneath the illuminated Bùi Viện arch at the street entrance with the evening street behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the neon and the crowd over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from across the road at one of the large Phố Đi Bộ Bùi Viện arches, while you stand at the arch so the arch and the street both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Vehicles still pass through at times, so keep clear of the carriageway while you shoot.
card.challenge: Catch the street in motion: switch on Live Photos and see if you can get one frame where the crowd is a happy blur and you're the only one standing still.
card.good_to_know: Bùi Viện took its present name in 1955, after the 19th-century reformer and diplomat Bùi Viện. It was rebuilt as a walking street and opened on 20 August 2017, the city's second pedestrian street after Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard. The streets around it, including Đề Thám, Phạm Ngũ Lão and Đỗ Quang Đẩu, are nicknamed the 'Backpacker Quarter'.

card.hook: Picture 81 storeys of glass standing up out of a park lawn like a giant bundle of bamboo. Landmark 81 is so tall and slim that it's the one building in Ho Chi Minh City that looks good from almost any patch of grass.
card.stand_here: Head for the riverside central lawn in Vinhomes Central Park. From the park area, the tower is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-west, so face that way and let the lawn and water run up to its base.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tower in from the lawn. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then try 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the crown and upper floors.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, then tap the tower and slide it a touch darker to keep the sky blue and the top detailed.
card.best_time: Early morning is the quietest time in the park, and the light is soft. At dusk, Ong Cay Bridge gives you a lit-up foreground, and night mode helps in the dim light.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the bronze hunter-and-dog statue on the Vinhomes Central Park side, use the front camera and let the tower rise behind you. At dusk, try Ong Cay Bridge with the glowing tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the park's pedestrian bridge to stand back at a distance, so the whole tower and its river reflection fit in the frame with you.
card.rules_and_safety: The park lawns are open public space, but check the official site before you go. The observation deck is a separate, ticketed attraction.
card.challenge: Crouch right down, tilt your phone up and see if you can make the tower look even taller than 461 metres.
card.good_to_know: Landmark 81 is the tallest building in Vietnam, at 461.2 metres and 81 storeys. Its shape is partly inspired by a bundle of bamboo sticks, a symbol of strength in Vietnamese culture. It was finished in April 2018, and the lower floors hold a shopping mall with an observation deck near the top.

card.hook: Picture a Huey helicopter, a fighter jet and a tank all parked in one walled yard, and you're allowed to walk right up to them. That's the courtyard at the War Remnants Museum, and it's where most visitors take their photos.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon, in the front courtyard, the first outdoor area you reach at 28 Võ Văn Tần Street. Face the aircraft so the museum building fills the background.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit an aircraft and the museum building into one frame. Use zoom 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details like the rotor, the cockpit or the tank tracks.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put an aircraft on one side of the frame, and let the building fill the space behind it.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the tour groups arrive, when the light on the aircraft is better. Check the official site for current opening times.
card.selfie_here: Head to the outdoor courtyard next to the UH-1 Huey helicopter, the display guides call the most photographed object there. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the Huey over your shoulder. The courtyard is also the only part of the site with decent natural light.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the pavement on Võ Văn Tần Street while you stand at the entrance gate, with the museum's Vietnamese name sign above you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are banned inside the building, but sources disagree about the courtyard, so ask staff at the gate. Flash isn't allowed indoors, and the Agent Orange section on the third floor doesn't allow photos.
card.challenge: Get all three stars (the Huey, the F-5A fighter and the M48 Patton tank) each in its own frame with the museum behind it, then find one close-up detail on each.
card.good_to_know: The building was once the US military's intelligence headquarters. An earlier version of the museum opened in September 1975 under a different name, and it has been the War Remnants Museum since 1995. About half a million people visit each year, roughly two-thirds from abroad, so it can get busy. It's a serious place, so keep your photos respectful.

card.hook: Most people head straight for the big front view, but the quiet corner has a tiny octagonal pavilion with a curved tile roof, perched on a little mound like it's waiting for its close-up. It's usually calmer than the front, too.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai and Nam Kỳ Khởi Nghĩa, at the left (northwest) corner of the grounds, right next to the octagonal pavilion on its mound. Face south: the palace is that way, with green lawns rolling out behind the pavilion.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the pavilion, the lawns and the palace into one frame. Then switch to 1x for a tidier shot of the pavilion with the palace behind it, and try 2x or more to pick out details from a distance (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level so the palace doesn't look tilted, then tap the pavilion roof and slide a little darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can be harsh on the pale walls, so save your lunch break for the shade.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, head to the front lawn at the main entrance and pose beside tank 843 or 390 with the palace façade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold your phone a bit low so the building fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the front lawn facing the palace, while you pose by the tank in the foreground so the whole building fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine, but flash is restricted in some rooms, so follow the signs in each room. The road by the gate is busy, so don't stand too close to it. The grounds are a ticketed visit, so check the official site for tickets and opening times before you go.
card.challenge: Put the pavilion roof in the foreground, slightly off-centre, and make the palace peek out behind it like it's hiding. Bonus points if your horizon stays dead level.
card.good_to_know: Independence Palace, also called Reunification Hall, was designed by the architect Ngô Viết Thụ. Building began on 1 July 1962 and the hall was inaugurated on 31 October 1966. It's best known as the place where a North Vietnamese tank came through the main gate at 10:45 on 30 April 1975, ending the Vietnam War. Today it's a museum and a hall for state events.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai and Nam Kỳ Khởi Nghĩa, at the left (northwest) corner of the grounds, right next to the octagonal pavilion on its mound. Face south: the palace is that way, with green lawns rolling out behind the pavilion.

card.hook: Picture a bronze statue, a ribbon of flowerbeds and a big yellow French-style City Hall glowing behind them. That's the postcard shot of Nguyễn Huệ, and you can grab it in about a minute.
card.stand_here: Stand at the north end of Nguyễn Huệ, in front of the People's Committee Building, right by the Ho Chi Minh statue. Face the statue and City Hall so the flowerbeds fill the bottom of your photo.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the statue, flowerbeds and City Hall together. If the square is busy, tap 0.5x to take in the whole front of the building. For the clock tower, try 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the statue a little off-centre, so the City Hall fills the space behind it.
card.best_time: Weekend evenings are lively because the whole boulevard is closed to cars, but the statue area gets crowded. For a clearer view of the statue and City Hall, try early in the day on a weekday. At Tết the street becomes the Flower Street, so expect a very different scene.
card.selfie_here: Try the fountain at the start of the walking street, with the skyscrapers behind you. Use your front camera and hold it a bit low so the high-rises fit over your shoulder. For a view of the whole boulevard, go up to a balcony at the Cafe Apartments, 42 Nguyễn Huệ. The top floors have The Letter Coffee, which has a balcony view of the street, though it depends on which floor you can reach.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the outer edge of the flowerbed directly in front of the statue, and ask a passer-by to crouch a little and shoot upward, so the City Hall clock tower sits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't climb on the statue's base. The street is crowded, so keep an eye on your bag and phone.
card.challenge: Get the statue, the flowers and the clock tower in one frame without a single stranger's head in it. Good luck, and be patient!
card.good_to_know: Nguyễn Huệ began as a canal, which was filled in during 1886–1887 and became a boulevard. It turned into a pedestrian street in 2015. For a second view, walk down to Bach Dang Wharf Park at the river end, which looks across the water to the skyline and the Bitexco Financial Tower.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the north end of Nguyễn Huệ, in front of the People's Committee Building, right by the Ho Chi Minh statue. Face the statue and City Hall so the flowerbeds fill the bottom of your photo.

card.hook: Scooters buzz past your elbow, but the building in front of you has been watching this corner since 1925. It's one of the best old buildings on the Saigon riverfront, so it makes a great first stop for a colonial-style street shot.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Đồng Khởi Street and Tôn Đức Thắng Street, at the junction facing the river, in front of the hotel's main frontage. The hotel lies to the west and is about 1 minute on foot away, so face west and you'll see it head-on with the river side of the building beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole frontage in from the corner, because you're close and the building fills the frame fast. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for facade details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's edges with them so the facade doesn't lean, and keep the whole roofline in the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows. After dark, try night mode and hold your phone steady against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Bach Dang pier on the riverbank across from the Majestic. Stand with the water in front of you so the hotel is at your back, then use the front camera at 0.5x to squeeze it in over your shoulder. Saigon Riverside Park, across the road from the hotel, should work the same way, but check the view on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the cafe side of the street, across from the hotel, to take the shot while you stand in front of the hotel.
card.rules_and_safety: The river road is busy with heavy traffic and noise, so wait for a gap before stepping back, and keep clear of the kerb. The outside is easy to photograph from the public street, but the hotel is a private business, so check its official site first if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the roofline sits perfectly level with a gridline, with no leaning and no scooter in the frame (good luck with the scooter).
card.good_to_know: The Majestic first opened in 1925 as a three-storey French colonial hotel with 44 bedrooms, with some Art Deco and classical French Riviera influence. Đồng Khởi Street, beside it, used to be called Rue Catinat. The hotel was renovated in Neo-Renaissance style in 1994 and is now a five-star hotel owned by Saigontourist Group.

The hotel lies to the west and is about 1 minute on foot away, so face west and you'll see it head-on with the river side of the building beside it.

card.hook: Scooters stream past, the crossing never really stops, and the Rex Hotel just sits on its corner looking calm about it. That's what makes it fun to photograph: you can see the whole building at once.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Nguyễn Huệ and Lê Thánh Tôn, on the corner facing the hotel's frontage. The hotel is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot, so face south-east towards its corner frontage.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole building. If it won't all fit, tap 0.5x. To home in on the signage or the upper floors, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sign, then slide the picture a touch darker so the lettering doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer, so you get a clearer view of the building. After dark the lit-up signage gives a totally different mood, but the junction is busy then, so use night mode and rest your phone against a wall or post.
card.selfie_here: Head to Nguyễn Huệ walking street at the Rex Hotel corner with Lê Thánh Tôn. Stand in the open street with the hotel's Nguyễn Huệ frontage behind you, use the front camera (tap 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the hotel over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by in front of Ho Chi Minh City Hall and pose at the Lê Thánh Tôn–Nguyễn Huệ corner, so the whole hotel shows behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the façade from the public street. The hotel and its arcade are commercial premises, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Catch a scooter whizzing through the foreground while the whole hotel stays in frame. Bonus points if the sign is still readable!
card.good_to_know: The building dates from 1927 and began as a two-storey car showroom and garage for a French businessman, showing Citroën and other European cars. During the Vietnam War it hosted daily US military press briefings that journalists nicknamed "The Five O'Clock Follies", and its rooftop bar was a well-known meeting place for officials and war correspondents. It has carried the Rex name again since 1986.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Nguyễn Huệ and Lê Thánh Tôn, on the corner facing the hotel's frontage. The hotel is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot, so face south-east towards its corner frontage.

card.hook: Plenty of people will tell you Gustave Eiffel built this pale yellow beauty. He didn't, and that makes a great caption. It's still a working post office, with a big clock keeping an eye on the square.
card.stand_here: Stand in Công xã Paris (Paris Commune Square), across the square from the facade, toward the cathedral side. Face the post office so the whole yellow front, with its clock and arched windows, fits in your frame next to the cathedral.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x from across the square for the full facade. Switch to 2x or higher to pick out the clock and the entrance arch. If you're stuck close to the building, 0.5x will fit it all in, but the edges will lean, so go easy on it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the building's edges so the walls stay straight, then tap the facade and slide it a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the yellow.
card.best_time: Go before 9am. The light hits the facade from the left and makes it look warmer, and it's likely to be quieter too. The entrance gets busy with tour groups, so take your wide shot first and move closer afterwards.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the main entrance with the yellow facade and clock behind you, front camera on, and hold it a little low so the clock makes it into the shot. If you go inside, the row of wooden phone booths on the left side of the hall makes a fun vintage backdrop. Stand in front of them with the booths behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of the square near the cathedral gates, while you stand in front of the post office so they can frame the full facade.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed inside the main hall, but it's a working building, so check the official site for opening times and rules before you go. Near the curb, keep a firm grip on your phone, because snatch-and-grab by motorbike riders is a known risk.
card.challenge: Walk along the outside wall and find the small plaques honouring Morse, Ampere, Volta, Ohm and Faraday, then get all five names in one photo.
card.good_to_know: The post office was built between 1886 and 1891, when Vietnam was part of French Indochina, and it mixes Gothic, Renaissance and French influences. It was designed by Alfred Foulhoux, not Eiffel. Inside, look for two painted maps from 1892: one of telegraph lines in southern Vietnam and Cambodia, and one of Saigon and its surroundings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Công xã Paris (Paris Commune Square), across the square from the facade, toward the cathedral side. Face the post office so the whole yellow front, with its clock and arched windows, fits in your frame next to the cathedral.

card.hook: Picture a grand French theatre sitting at the end of a busy Saigon street, with motorbikes streaming past like it's no big deal. Early in the morning, that street goes quiet and the building gets its moment.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement of Đồng Khởi street and face west, looking down the road toward the front of the Opera House. The classic shot is taken from the middle of the road, but that's risky, so only use it if traffic is completely clear. Otherwise stay on the pavement.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the street leading to the façade. If you're close and the whole front won't fit, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the carved reliefs, balustrades and arched windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the central entrance on the middle vertical line so the building looks perfectly balanced.
card.best_time: Go around 7:30 AM, when the road is clear of heavy traffic and it's quietest. The sky can be bright then, so if the stonework looks washed out, tap the façade and make it a touch darker.
card.selfie_here: Climb to the top step of the entrance stairs after sunset. Use your front camera, turn your back to the lit façade and face Nguyen Hue Walking Street, so the glowing building sits behind you. It's a local tip rather than an official one.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the park across Đồng Khởi Street, directly opposite the Opera House, while you pose on the entrance steps, so they can frame the whole façade with you in it.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside is fine to photograph from the pavements, but the interior needs a show ticket and photos aren't allowed during performances. The junction is full of motorbikes, so shoot from the pavement, not the road. At night, stick to the well-lit pavements around Lam Son Square.
card.challenge: Get a symmetrical shot with the entrance dead centre on your gridline and not one motorbike in the frame. Check the edges before you tap!
card.good_to_know: The Opera House is a French colonial theatre, finished by 1 January 1900. Its ornate façade is shaped like the Petit Palais in France, built the same year. Some of the original decoration came off in 1943 and part of it went back on when the façade was restored in 1998. Today it seats 500, though it once held up to 1,800.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement of Đồng Khởi street and face west, looking down the road toward the front of the Opera House. The classic shot is taken from the middle of the road, but that's risky, so only use it if traffic is completely clear. Otherwise stay on the pavement.

card.hook: Two landmarks, one open square, and a steady stream of scooters trying to photobomb you. The Continental's colonial corner sits right beside the Opera House, and you can get both in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on Quảng trường Lam Sơn (Lam Sơn Square), beside the Opera House. Face back across the square towards the hotel's corner with Đồng Khởi Street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the hotel corner and the Opera House together. If they won't both fit, tap 0.5x. Use 2x or higher for close-ups of balconies and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the hotel corner on one vertical line and let the Opera House fill the other side, then hold your phone level so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the square. Check the light on the day, because the facade can be in shade or glare depending on the hour. For selfies, go after dark when the building is lit.
card.selfie_here: Head to the open forecourt in front of the hotel at 132 Dong Khoi Street and stand with the facade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more of the building over your shoulder, and aim for after dark when it's lit up.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from a spot in the forecourt that keeps the whole facade in frame, while you pose in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: The hotel is a working hotel, so check its official site before you go inside. Photos in public areas like the lobby and bar are generally fine, but private rooms or long shoots need permission. The inner courtyard is inside the hotel and may not be open to non-guests.
card.challenge: Take your shot with zero scooters in the frame. Fire off a few in a row and see how long it takes you to get a clean one.
card.good_to_know: The Continental was built in 1878, opened in 1880, and is generally described as the oldest hotel in Vietnam. It's named after the Hôtel Continental in Paris. During the First Indochina War it was nicknamed Radio Catinat because journalists and politicians met there. Graham Greene stayed here, and it appears in The Quiet American and in the 1992 film Indochine.

card.hook: Stand at the bottom of Bitexco and look up, and 6,000 panels of glass seem to sweep into the sky like a lotus petal. Your neck will complain, but your photos will thank you.
card.stand_here: Walk to the phone icon on the map, right at the foot of Bitexco Financial Tower in Saigon's Financial District. Face the tower and tilt your phone up a little.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x at the foot of the tower to fit its full height in. Walk back a little and switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched view. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the helipad and the crown.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines, so it stands tall instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is your sweet spot, when the glass picks up warm colour and the city lights come on. Midday sun makes the glass look flat and bright.
card.selfie_here: Try the plaza at the tower's foot, facing the Hồ Tùng Mậu side. It shows the whole curved, lotus-like shape without you stepping far back, so use the front camera and let the tower fill the frame over your shoulder. The Bach Dang Wharf riverside walkway is another open spot with a clear view of the tower. Neither is a official selfie spot, so check your framing on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Van Don quay on the Khánh Hội side of the river gives the full side profile of the tower with the helipad, so it's a good place for a passer-by to take the wide shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Phone snatching by passing motorbikes happens on Ton Duc Thang and Nguyen Hue, so hold your phone on the side away from the road. The observation deck and other parts of the building may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the helipad sticking out like a lotus bud, then zoom in and get it with a tree or lamp at the edge of the frame.
card.good_to_know: Bitexco is a 68-floor glass tower, 262.5 metres tall. When it was finished in 2010 it was the tallest building in Vietnam, and today it's the second tallest in Ho Chi Minh City. Architect Carlos Zapata took the lotus, Vietnam's national flower, as his inspiration. There's an observation deck on the 49th floor if you want the city view too.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the phone icon on the map, right at the foot of Bitexco Financial Tower in Saigon's Financial District. Face the tower and tilt your phone up a little.

card.hook: Those red bricks sailed all the way from Toulouse in France, and 140-odd years later they still glow like they're showing off. This is the cathedral everyone wants in their Saigon photos, and you're about to get yours.
card.stand_here: Stand in Công trường Công xã Paris, the square in front of the facade, with the white statue of Our Lady of Peace in the foreground. The cathedral is to the west of you, so face it and keep the statue low in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to try fitting the statue and both towers into one shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer view, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the statue's face, the brickwork or the tops of the towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the statue up with the gap between the two towers, then tap the red brick so it looks rich and warm.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is warmest on the red brick. Check on the day whether scaffolding is covering the front.
card.selfie_here: Head into the small garden beside the Our Lady of Peace statue in Paris Commune Square, with the cathedral behind you (the statue faces the roundabout). Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt the phone so the towers peek over your shoulder. For something different, walk round to the side of the building and pose in front of the massive main doors.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the front of the square, where the statue and the twin-towered church fit in one frame, while you stand in the statue garden.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones need permission and are generally not allowed here. Don't photograph people at prayer. The interior has been closed during renovation, so stay on the outside grounds and square, and check the current status before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the white statue sitting perfectly in the gap between the two towers, with no stranger's head in the way?
card.good_to_know: The walls went up between 1877 and 1880, and the bricks came from Toulouse. The two towers were added in 1895 and are about 58 metres tall. The statue was installed in 1959, and the cathedral has been called Notre-Dame since then. Restoration is expected to finish around 2027.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Công trường Công xã Paris, the square in front of the facade, with the white statue of Our Lady of Peace in the foreground. The cathedral is to the west of you, so face it and keep the statue low in your frame.

card.hook: You might walk straight past this place, because the entrance hides under shady trees and is easy to miss from the street. Once you're through, the coral-pink walls hit you all at once.
card.stand_here: Stand in the open front yard of the Jade Emperor Pagoda, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the main hall so the whole pink front is ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the front of the main hall. If the courtyard feels tight, tap 0.5x to fit the whole building in. Then try 2x to 5x to pick out the roof decorations and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pink wall, then drag the slider to make it a little darker if the bright sky is washing out the roof decorations.
card.best_time: Late afternoon gives warm light on the walls. Early morning is quieter, with fewer people in your shot. Expect crowds during Tet and on the 9th day of the first lunar month.
card.selfie_here: Head to the front yard by the turtle pond and turn around so the pagoda facade is behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the pink front over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the front yard across from the building, back from the pond edge, so your whole pink facade and roofline fit in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so cover your shoulders and knees and follow any signs. Photos inside the halls are restricted or unclear, so treat the courtyard as your main spot. Keep flash off, ask before photographing anyone praying, and don't photograph people at the fertility shrine. Keep your phone clear of incense smoke.
card.challenge: Find one carved detail or roof decoration you'd have missed at 1x, zoom in to 5x, and see if a friend can guess where it is.
card.good_to_know: The temple mixes Taoist, Buddhist and Confucian traditions. It's also called Chùa Ngọc Hoàng, and since 1984 its Buddhist name has been Phước Hải Tự, meaning "Luck Sea Temple". It was founded by Liu Daoyuan, a Cantonese merchant who had migrated to the city, and Barack Obama visited on 22 May 2016.

card.hook: Before you've seen a single giraffe, the red-roofed arch of the Sở Thú gate tells you exactly where you are. Big leafy trees rise behind it, and it makes a great first photo of the day.
card.stand_here: Stand on the street at the corner of Nguyễn Bỉnh Khiêm and Lê Duẩn, by the main gate of Saigon Zoo and Botanical Gardens. Face the gate so the arch, the sign and the treetops all fit in one frame.
card.zoom: If you're close to the gate, start at zoom 0.5x to get the arch, sign and trees in together. If you can step back across the street, 1x looks more natural with less stretching at the edges. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the roof and sign.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the gate on the central vertical line so the arch looks symmetrical, and keep your phone level so the roofline doesn't tilt.
card.best_time: Early morning is worth a try, as the light is softer and the gate should be quieter. If people wander into your shot, wait a moment, or keep a few in the frame to show how big the gate is.
card.selfie_here: Guides name the Orchid House, where rare Vietnamese orchids are displayed, as a must-snap stop. They also say the giraffe zone makes for adorable selfies. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone so the orchids or giraffes are over your shoulder. No guide says which way to face, so check the framing on your screen before you smile.
card.ask_someone: On the main avenue lined with century-old trees, ask a passer-by to take a wide shot of you with the trees stretching away behind.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed in the zoo, but keep flash off around the animals. Keep an eye on young children near animal enclosures and water features. Entry is likely ticketed and has set hours, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the gate perfectly symmetrical with a dead-straight roofline, then add one person walking through the frame to show how big it is.
card.good_to_know: Admiral Pierre-Paul de La Grandière commissioned the zoo in 1864, and it opened to the public in 1869, making it one of the oldest continuously operating zoos in the world. It has roughly 590 animals of 125 species and about 1,830 trees and plants of 260 species, some over 100 years old. Inside you'll also find the Ho Chi Minh City Museum of History and a temple to the Hùng Kings, which began life as a memorial to soldiers.

card.hook: Yes, the whole church really is pink, and it's even pinker in real life than in your friend's photos. Locals call it the pink church, and one look across the street tells you why.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement at the corner of Hai Bà Trưng and Đinh Công Tráng, on the side where Cộng Cà Phê is. The church is across the road to the south, about 1 minute on foot from its gate, so face south and you'll see the whole facade and bell tower.
card.zoom: Start at 1x from across the road to fit the whole facade and the tower. If the pavement is crowded and the tower won't fit, switch to 0.5x. Use 2x for the tower top and the arches.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pink wall, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the pink doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the facade glows. One guide suggests about 3:00 to 4:30 pm.
card.selfie_here: Go to the church plaza just inside the white arched front gates and turn your back on the church, so the pink facade and bell tower are behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if the tower won't fit, and enjoy the blue sky and green trees. For a close-up portrait, the long pink tiled wall along the right-hand side of the grounds is a dreamy backdrop that gets good sunlight.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement across Hai Bà Trưng (the side street Đinh Công Tráng beside Cộng Cà Phê works too) while you stand in front of the church, so the whole facade fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't step into the road for the shot. Motorbikes pass very close, so shoot from the pavement. Opening times vary and the interior is for worshippers during mass, so check locally before you go. One page says photography isn't allowed inside the church.
card.challenge: Crouch low, tilt the phone up, and get the tower standing tall on a gridline, with a friend off to one side for scale.
card.good_to_know: The church's formal name is the Church of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. It was completed on 16 December 1876, in the French colonial period, and it's the second-largest church in Ho Chi Minh City after Notre-Dame Basilica. The whole building, outside and in, has been painted pastel pink since 1957. One guide mentions possible restoration work on the outside walls, which could affect the view.

card.hook: Walk down Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard and the whole street seems to point at one thing: a big yellow-and-white City Hall with a clock tower, sitting dead centre at the far end. It's the easiest symmetrical photo you'll take all trip.
card.stand_here: Stand on Nguyễn Huệ Walking Street, right on the centre line of the boulevard, and face the north-west end where City Hall closes the view. Keep the bronze Ho Chi Minh statue in front of you, and if the building won't fit, walk a few steps back along the street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the facade, clock tower and statue all in one. If you're too close, try zoom 0.5x. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is good for the clock tower and the little Marianne sculptures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the clock tower up with the middle vertical line, with the statue low in the frame and the tower above it.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light on the facade is softer. Come back in the evening once the building is lit, and use night mode, holding the phone steady against your body or a rail.
card.selfie_here: Try the flower garden beside the bronze statue on the Ho Chi Minh statue plaza, with the yellow City Hall facade behind you. Use the front camera (or zoom 0.5x if your phone allows it on the front) and hold it low so the clock tower rises over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the centre line a few steps back from the statue, with City Hall behind you, and ask a passer-by to shoot from farther back along the boulevard so the whole building shows.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't wander into restricted areas or get in the way of government activity, and skip the drone, as drones are generally restricted around government buildings here. It gets busy with pedestrians in the evening, so keep an eye on your valuables.
card.challenge: Find all three Marianne sculptures under the pediments, then zoom in and get one clean shot of them.
card.good_to_know: The French began building City Hall in 1898 and it opened in 1909, designed by Fernand Gardè, who borrowed ideas from the Paris town hall and the bell towers of northern France. A second storey was added to the wings in the 1940s. It's still the working home of the city's People's Committee and People's Council, so the inside is generally closed. Check current opening arrangements if you hope to go in.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Nguyễn Huệ Walking Street, right on the centre line of the boulevard, and face the north-west end where City Hall closes the view. Keep the bronze Ho Chi Minh statue in front of you, and if the building won't fit, walk a few steps back along the street.

card.hook: Picture a flash of red and orange tucked between glass towers and shopfronts in the middle of District 1. That's Mariamman Temple, and the clash with the city around it is exactly why it looks so good on your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on Đường Trương Định, on the opposite side of the street from the main entrance of Mariamman Temple (number 45). The temple is about 26 m to the south-west of there, so face it square-on and let the tall gopuram rise above the doorway.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole frontage. If scooters or the narrow pavement stop you stepping back, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the statues on the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn your gridlines on to keep the gopuram upright, then tap the facade and slide it a touch darker so the reds and oranges stay rich.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and lighter traffic. It still works at any daylight hour, so don't stress if you turn up at noon.
card.selfie_here: Head into the forecourt in front of the main gopuram entrance, facing out toward Trương Định street, which is the courtyard and frontage area guides name as the popular photo spot. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and tilt up so the colourful gopuram sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far pavement of Trương Định Street, opposite the main entrance, while you stand in the forecourt, so the gopuram fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working place of worship. Photos are fine in the outer areas, but ask before photographing worshippers or going near the sanctum, and don't photograph the main altar during active worship. Keep flash off, dress modestly and leave the drone at home.
card.challenge: Catch the whole gopuram with not a single scooter in the shot. Patience wins, so wait for the gap!
card.good_to_know: Mariamman Temple is a small Hindu temple dedicated to the goddess Mariamman. The Nagarathar, a trading community from Tamil Nadu in India, built it in the late 19th century. The gopuram above the entrance is about 12 m high and carries a number of statues. Admission is free.

card.hook: Most people walk past a seven-storey bell tower without a second look, but this one is hard to miss, rising right beside the gate with the pagoda entrance tucked behind it. Stand on the pavement and you get the whole scene in one tidy shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement on Bà Huyện Thanh Quan, right in front of the main gate. The pagoda is just to the south-west of you, so face that way to line up the bell tower with the entrance behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the straight-on view of tower, gate and entrance. If the pavement is too narrow to fit the whole tower, drop to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to pick out the entrance or the Quan Âm statue from the same spot.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines, put the bell tower on one of the vertical lines and keep your phone level so the tower doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Opening times can change, and the sources we checked don't agree, so check before you go. Festival days get crowded, so a quieter day should give you a cleaner picture.
card.selfie_here: Just inside the gate, stand next to the Chinese-style Quan Âm statue in the garden courtyard, with the pagoda behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder. The front stairs leading up to the main hall are a second spot, with the main hall behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The gate and garden can be photographed from outside. Ask permission before photographing monks, other people or the interiors, and don't use flash in the prayer hall. It's a working place of worship, so keep it quiet and respectful, and watch your belongings on busy festival days.
card.challenge: Take the bell tower with no lean at all, then walk in and zoom 2x on the Quan Âm statue for a matching shot.
card.good_to_know: Xá Lợi is the largest pagoda in Ho Chi Minh City, on a plot of about 5,000 square metres in District 3. Building began in 1956 and it opened in 1958 to house a sample of relics of the Buddha, which is where its name comes from. In 1963 it became known as one of the Buddhist pagodas raided during that year's protests.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement on Bà Huyện Thanh Quan, right in front of the main gate. The pagoda is just to the south-west of you, so face that way to line up the bell tower with the entrance behind it.

card.hook: The Saigon Central Mosque is a little white and blue building that looks like it got squeezed in between the towers. That's exactly why it makes a great photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Đông Du, on the stretch in front of the mosque, and face the Sheraton and the city towers. From there the mosque is to the north-west of you, with the towers rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the mosque and the towers in one frame. Try 2x if your phone has it, because it makes the towers look closer to the mosque. Use 0.5x only if you're tight against the street, and keep the phone level so the minarets don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the mosque, then drag the slider a touch darker so the white walls keep their detail instead of turning pale.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white walls and less glare. Go whenever the street is quietest.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you need more room, and turn so the mosque sits over your shoulder. Hold the phone level so the minarets don't tilt, and take a few frames because people and vehicles keep passing.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a place of worship, and public access can vary, so check on the day. Take your photos from outside on the street, and ask before taking any pictures inside. Traffic is constant, so wait for a gap before you step back to compose.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the mosque on the lower third with the towers filling the sky, and catch one frame with no scooter cutting across the front.
card.good_to_know: Building began on 21 December 1934 and the mosque was completed in 1935. It was first known as the India Jamia Muslim Mosque, and JM Mohamed Ismael, who headed the British Indian Muslim community, led the project. It's described as Roman in style, has four minarets, and was visited by Jawaharlal Nehru and Indira Gandhi in October 1954.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Đông Du, on the stretch in front of the mosque, and face the Sheraton and the city towers. From there the mosque is to the north-west of you, with the towers rising behind it.

selfie_research.notes: No selfie spot was found. None of the pages I checked names a specific vantage point with the mosque behind a visitor. They give only general advice, such as the exterior against the city backdrop (Airial, 'Saigon Central Mosque (2025)'), and a review about looking up at the minarets with high-rise buildings (Tripadvisor, 'Historic Mosque' review). Pages name the address as 66 Dong Du Street, Dist 1 (Vietfuntravel, 'Saigon Central Mosque'; Tripadvisor listing). Because the brief requires a named place, I left both spot fields empty rather than invent one. A photo-permission point is in the sources, but it is not a selfie-stick or tripod rule, so I left it out of 'rules'. Vietfuntravel and BestPriceTravel ('Saigon Central Mosque Ho Chi Minh City: Travel Information 2026') both say to ask permission before taking photographs. The sources also disagree on access: BestPriceTravel says non-Muslims may not enter, while Wendy Wei Tours says Muslims may enter on Fridays and tourists can appreciate the facade in the morning. No safety point was stated on any page I found.
